channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Day ten at Boston Scientific: shipping starts to come back, manufacturing has not, and no controller was ever touched
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Ten days after detecting an intrusion on 25 August, Boston Scientific is beginning to claw operations back rather than declaring them restored. The company says it aims to partially resume shipping for some products, then ramp order processing and dispatch to full capacity once the environment is validated; manufacturing, order intake and global shipping remain disrupted meanwhile, with EDI and GHX orders queuing and production shifts cancelled at Irish plants. Its latest update reports no malicious activity seen since detection, confines the access to certain on-premise systems, and leaves cloud services, implanted cardiac devices and established remote monitoring unaffected. No entry route, vulnerability or ransomware claim has been named. For OT defenders that absence is the point: nothing here reached a PLC, yet a compromise of the systems that tell a plant what to build and where to ship it has held production down for a fortnight. - Boston Scientific incident page and SEC filing, plus SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber recovery reporting — also covered by MedTech Dive, Supply Chain Dive, TechCrunch and CBS News - Detected 25 Aug 2026; disclosed 26 Aug 2026; manufacturing disruption confirmed 28 Aug 2026; company update 30 Aug 2026; still recovering with partial shipping restoration targeted, per reporting through 3 Sep 2026 — re-verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] The water campaign, quantified: CISA counts 100-plus internet-exposed systems hit, with controller logic and alarms altered
item.category: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, water sector; CISA-quantified scale
item.description: CISA has put a figure on July’s campaign against US water utilities: malicious activity against more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector, commonly programmable logic controllers wired straight into a cellular modem. The FBI records incidents at utilities in at least seven states since 27 July, with reporting placing targeting across at least a dozen. Some degraded operations — lost pressure, flooding, plants run by hand — though supply was not widely interrupted, and in several intrusions actors altered controllers to disable shutdown processes and alarms, letting unsafe conditions develop unannounced. US officials assess Iranian actors as likely responsible and describe the activity as largely opportunistic. It stays on the page five weeks on because of the admission behind the number: the exposure that carried it was in nobody’s asset register. - CISA exposure-reduction guidance and the FBI/EPA public service announcement — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Cybersecurity Dive, TechCrunch and The Register; Minnesota impact detail from state officials and SecurityWeek - Scale confirmed and reported 26 Aug 2026; observed activity July 2026; FBI PSA issued 30 Jul 2026 — re-verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] Attackers walked from a wind farm’s firewall to another plant’s PLCs across a shared cellular APN — and stopped a turbine
item.category: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, energy; first documented private-APN pivot
item.description: CERT Polska’s follow-up report on attacks against Poland’s energy sector documents an intrusion path that maps almost exactly onto the exposure CISA and the NCSC are now warning about, and it is the reason this older item belongs on the page. Attackers compromised a FortiGate firewall at a wind farm, moved to a Teltonika cellular router, and then crossed a private cellular APN that had been provisioned without client isolation — meaning every SIM on that APN could reach every other. On the far side sat a WAGO PFC200 at a separate combined heat and power plant, still carrying default administrator credentials, which the attackers used to build an SSH bridge into the OT network. From there they forced three Siemens PLCs into STOP and set password protection on them, shutting down a steam turbine and the process-water treatment serving a town of roughly 50,000 people. CERT Polska assesses this as the first documented real-world OT intrusion via lateral movement across a private APN, and notes the shared-APN-without-isolation configuration is common in Poland and likely well beyond it. - CERT Polska energy-sector incident follow-up report, as reported by BleepingComputer — corroborated by SecurityWeek - Report published 10 Aug 2026; underlying incident occurred 2025 — verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] A small UK generating station ran manually for four days after an Iran-linked cyberattack
item.category: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, power generation (UK)
item.description: A small British power generating station was taken offline for four days by a cyberattack, with staff forced to restore operations manually. The Telegraph broke the story on 22 August; the UK government confirmed that a small-scale generator had been affected while stating there was at no point a risk to the national energy system, and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has since contacted power companies about the risk. UK assessments reported by the Telegraph point to hackers affiliated with the Iranian regime, likely the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The site’s size is the uncomfortable part rather than a reassurance: distributed generation, embedded generators and behind-the-meter assets sit below most reporting thresholds, are often remotely operated by a third party, and are numerous enough that an attack that works once is repeatable. - SecurityWeek and CNBC, both citing the originating Telegraph report and the UK government statement - Incident occurred July 2026; reported 22–23 Aug 2026; government response reported 24 Aug 2026 — re-verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [High] A water-sector PLC maker was ransomed, and roughly 200 of its SCADA systems are reachable from the internet
item.category: Supply chain — Micro-Comm, water/wastewater PLC and SCADA supplier
item.description: Micro-Comm of Olathe, Kansas — which builds programmable logic controllers and the SCADAview CSX platform used by water and wastewater utilities — discovered a breach on 31 July and confirmed it publicly on 26 August, with the FBI investigating. The Barracuda ransomware group, a profit-motivated crew that says it is not state sponsored, published what it claims are nearly 850,000 stolen files totalling about 644 GB. Researchers reviewing the file listing report references to municipal customers, a US military facility, employee names and product documentation including system diagrams. The FBI has told the company it assesses the intrusion as opportunistic rather than targeted, and no manipulation of any customer’s control system has been reported. The number that should hold a water operator’s attention is a separate one: roughly 200 SCADAview CSX systems across US states are reachable from the public internet — the same exposure pattern that carried July’s campaign into more than 100 water systems. - Reuters exclusive of 26 Aug 2026 carrying company and FBI confirmation — corroborated by IBTimes and Newsmax; internet-exposure figure attributed to researchers cited in the reporting - Breach discovered 31 Jul 2026; disclosed 26 Aug 2026 — re-verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] NCSC: OT targeting is up across sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
item.category: Agency warning — Cross-sector OT targeting, real-world disruption
item.description: The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre published a statement on 27 August saying it is seeing increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors worldwide, including in the UK, carried out by a range of threat actors, and that this has already produced limited real-world disruption. The agency ties it to a broader pattern of disruptive activity against internet-exposed systems and edge devices — routers, gateways and firewalls that hand an attacker a foothold. Its asks are concrete: keep an accurate inventory of internet-facing systems, understand what each edge device does and where its data flows, patch promptly, retire end-of-life equipment, disable Telnet and SNMP v1/v2, and watch for unexpected configuration changes or outbound connections. Coming a day after CISA’s exposure guidance, this is two national agencies independently reaching the same conclusion in the same week. - UK NCSC news statement — corroborated by GovInfoSecurity and CircleID - Published 27 Aug 2026 — re-verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] Five agencies say the S7 family is being actively hunted — and that the exploit scripts are being written with AI
item.category: NSA/CISA/FBI/DOE/EPA joint advisory AA26-231A — active targeting of Siemens S7 series PLCs
item.description: The joint advisory published on 19 August is the primary-source anchor under this edition’s AI research. The NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA report threat actors actively working against Siemens S7 controllers that are internet-exposed or poorly segmented, spanning the S7‑200, ‑300, ‑400, ‑1200 and ‑1500 lines, and name Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Water and Wastewater, Chemical, Food and Agriculture and Commercial Facilities as the most affected sectors. What makes it notable is the method: the agencies describe AI‑generated reconnaissance and exploitation scripts built around the open-source python‑snap7 library and disguised to look like legitimate OT monitoring tooling. Two familiar conditions do the enabling — internet exposure through weak segmentation, and default or weak credentials. The protocol expertise that used to gate ICS exploit development is no longer the barrier. - CISA joint advisory AA26-231A (NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE, EPA) — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Tenable and Infosecurity Magazine - Published 19 Aug 2026 — re-verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [High] Eighteen frontier models were run at a real enterprise network. One completed the whole kill chain unaided.
item.category: Booz Allen Cyber Weapon Index — measured offensive capability of frontier AI models
item.description: Booz Allen published its Cyber Weapon Index on 4 September, testing eighteen US and Chinese frontier AI models against a production-grade enterprise network. One — Anthropic’s Claude Mythos — autonomously executed a full cyber kill chain, both starting from a stolen employee credential and, in the harder run, with no credentials at all. Roughly two-thirds of the models tested reliably gained initial access to a defended network without credentials, and the firm expects most to reach full autonomous kill-chain capability within about six months. The finding defenders should hold onto is the one the headline buries: every frontier API model scored zero against real, previously unknown vulnerabilities. Strong performance came against flaws deliberately introduced for the test. Booz Allen also reports that the “attack harness” — the tooling, memory and autonomy wrapped around a model — matters as much as the model, so cheap engineering can lift a weaker model close to frontier performance. None of the testing was OT-specific. - Booz Allen Cyber Weapon Index / The Offensive Frontier: AI as the Attacker, via Industrial Cyber - Published 4 Sep 2026 — verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [High] A frontier model ported a working PLC exploit to a second controller in eight hours — then bricked it
item.category: Forescout Vedere Labs — AI-assisted exploit development against PLCs
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs published the result of a deliberately awkward experiment: point a frontier AI model at real industrial hardware and see how far it gets. Starting from the team’s own remote code execution exploit for a WAGO 750-852, built on CVE-2021-31886 — a pre-authentication overflow in the Nucleus FTP server — they asked Claude to port it to the related 750-831, giving the model a terminal, Ghidra and the physical device. It worked, but not cleanly. The first model tried failed to trace the vulnerable function; a stronger model eventually worked out why the injected shellcode was being wiped before it could run, and once past that it produced two working payloads in twelve minutes. Total cost of the final stage: over eight hours and more than $500 in API charges. A follow-up attempt at a command-and-control implant wrote to flash and permanently bricked the PLC. - Forescout Research – Vedere Labs report, via SecurityWeek — corroborated by Cybersecurity Dive with direct comment from Vedere Labs - CISA batch published 1 Sep 2026; Rockwell advisory round-up reported 2 Sep 2026 — verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [Medium] Modelled, not observed: compromise 29% of Britain’s battery fleet and the grid does not need to be attacked twice
item.category: Centrii GRIDLOCK report — modelled risk to grid-scale battery energy storage
item.description: Centrii’s GRIDLOCK report, published 3 September, runs a Monte Carlo model 10,000 times across three security postures and puts a 92% probability on a major coordinated attack against UK battery energy storage by 2031 under today’s industry-average practice — falling to 61% if IEC 62443 certification were mandatory. The mechanism is the interesting part for control engineers. An attacker does not need to stop generation; it needs to desynchronise the balancing layer. Cloud control platforms issue charge and discharge commands to thousands of units, so synchronised commands, or a few seconds of injected delay in response to grid signals, push frequency outside safe limits, protective relays trip in sequence, and the model has that cascading to a blackout inside two minutes. The scale required is smaller than owners assume: 400 units, about 29% of GB capacity, or 5.4% of the ERCOT fleet. It is a forecast, not an event. - Centrii GRIDLOCK report, via Industrial Cyber - Published 3 Sep 2026 — verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [Medium] Food and Ag-ISAC counts a 62% rise in sector ransomware — and names the inventory problem underneath it
item.category: Food and Ag-ISAC — sector threat report; ransomware, hacktivist OT targeting and “shadow OT”
item.description: The Food and Ag-ISAC’s State of the Threat report, released 3 September with the IT-ISAC, records 227 ransomware incidents against food and agriculture through July 2026 against 140 in the same period last year — a 62% rise, with Qilin (47), The Gentlemen (31) and Akira (14) most active, and the sector eighth most-targeted at roughly 5% of all tracked attacks. Most of it is opportunistic rather than aimed. Two findings travel beyond the sector. Hacktivist groups have moved from defacement and denial-of-service into internet-accessible HMIs, SCADA and automatic tank gauges, so a “hacktivist” label no longer implies low operational impact — several such personas have documented state links. And the report names the underlying problem directly: shadow OT, the networked silo sensors, automated feeders and cold-chain thermometers added for efficiency that never reach an IT asset register. - Food and Ag-ISAC / IT-ISAC State of the Threat: Food and Agriculture Sector Cyber Trends, via Industrial Cyber - Published 3 Sep 2026 — verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] CISA put SonicWall’s exploited SMA1000 pair in KEV a day after disclosure — a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw chained to code execution
item.category: SonicWall SMA1000 — Two zero-days exploited, CVSS 10 chain, now in CISA KEV
item.description: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance have been exploited in the wild, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2 September as part of a seven-CVE batch. CVE-2026-83548, carrying a CVSS score of 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface that lets an unauthenticated attacker reach sensitive functionality; CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an OS command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console that an authenticated attacker can turn into remote code execution. SonicWall says it observed exploitation of both, which points to the pair being chained for unauthenticated code execution on the appliance. The vendor found the flaws and the attacks internally, and has published no indicators of compromise. Models 6210, 7210 and 8200v are affected. For OT operators this is the exact class of device that vendor engineers, integrators and on-call staff use to reach the plant from outside — a box that sits at the boundary, terminates trusted sessions and is rarely covered by an OT change window. - SonicWall PSIRT advisory SNWLID-2026-0016 and the CISA KEV addition of 2 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek and Help Net Security - Advisory published 1 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 2 Sep 2026 — verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [High] CISA’s 3 September batch lands on the remote-access client itself — a CVSS 9.6 root-level flaw in IXON VPN
item.category: CISA ICS advisory batch — ICSA-26-246 series; industrial remote access, SCADA platform, engineering tooling
item.description: The five advisories CISA published on 3 September are worth reading in a particular order, because the first one sits on the exact attack path two national agencies spent last week warning about. ICSA-26-246-02 covers CVE-2026-75925 in the IXON VPN Client below 1.4.7, rated CVSS v3.1 9.6: the client’s local configuration interface accepts changes without authenticating the requester, and does not neutralise line-ending sequences before writing them to a file that a privileged subprocess later consumes — so an attacker can inject extra directives and have commands run as root or SYSTEM. The injected configuration survives reboots, and the VPN keeps working normally, so nothing about the machine’s behaviour tells the engineer using it that anything changed. This is the software sitting on maintenance laptops and engineering workstations that reach machines in the field. The rest of the batch is more routine but not trivial: ICSA-26-246-06 flags CVE-2026-77393 in Inductive Automation Ignition 8.1.53 and earlier at CVSS 8.8, where the Gateway’s Create Project Role(s) setting shipped blank and any authenticated user able to run gateway scripts can create projects; ICSA-26-246-03 covers CVE-2026-12663 in Rockwell ControlFLASH 15.07 and earlier, whose installer granted the Everyone group write access to a product directory; ICSA-26-246-01 covers CVE-2026-77477 in the OPC Foundation UA LocalDiscoveryServer installers; and ICSA-26-246-08 covers a missing-authorization issue, CVE-2026-82684, in Tycon Systems TPDIN-Monitor-WEB3 2.2.9 and earlier that could expose credentials, configuration or flash contents. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-246-01, -02, -03, -06 and -08 — summarised by the Viakoo/Security Boulevard daily OT briefing; IXON technical detail cross-checked against the vendor security advisory page and CVE records - Advisories published 3 Sep 2026 — verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [High] CISA’s 1 September batch is five-sixths Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
item.category: ICSA-26-244-01 to -05 + Rockwell PSIRT — a dozen-plus fixes, controllers included
item.description: CISA published eight ICS advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The set covers RSLinx Classic (ICSA-26-244-01), the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (-02), the Logix platform (-03), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). The RSLinx item is the one most sites will feel first: four flaws — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625 — let crafted Common Industrial Protocol traffic crash the communications service on version 4.50 and earlier, and it stays down until somebody restarts it by hand. RSLinx is the data path between controllers and the HMI, historian and engineering workstations, so a crash there is a visibility outage on a running process, not an IT inconvenience. The batch also carries an update to the Rockwell 1734 POINT I/O advisory (ICSA-26-202-09, Update A) and Update G to the long-running Mitsubishi Electric FA engineering software advisory (ICSA-24-135-04). Rockwell’s own round-up, reported 2 September, puts the total above a dozen fixes and adds detail the CISA summaries do not: remote code execution in FactoryTalk Historian, privilege escalation in FactoryTalk Activation Manager and in the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool, arbitrary code execution through the ControlFLASH firmware utility, cross-site scripting plus a web-server denial of service in ArmorStart distributed motor controllers, and further denial-of-service issues in 1756-ENBT and in Logix controllers via a third-party component. One item needs care rather than alarm: Rockwell’s advisory for CVE-2026-9637, a high-severity denial of service in ControlLogix and CompactLogix, is flagged as exploited in its document header but listed as not exploited in the body, and CISA states it is not aware of exploitation — read it as a documentation inconsistency, not a live campaign, and patch it on its merits. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-244-01 through -05 published 1 Sep 2026, plus ICSA-26-202-09 Update A and ICSA-24-135-04 Update G, read against the Rockwell Automation security advisory index and SecurityWeek’s 2 Sep 2026 round-up of the full Rockwell set - Published 1 Sep 2026 — verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [High] Cisco patches root-level flaws in the routers and switches that OT quietly depends on
item.category: Cisco PSIRT — three CVSS 9.8 flaws in IOS XR and Nexus 9000, 3 Sep 2026
item.description: Cisco released fixes on 3 September covering seven CVEs in IOS XR, two of which — CVE-2026-20274 and CVE-2026-20279 — carry a CVSS score of 9.8, plus a third at the same score, CVE-2026-20212, in Nexus 9000 series switches. The reported condition is the kind that removes every intermediate step from an attack chain: a remote, unauthenticated attacker can reach TCP ports that listen by default and execute code with root privileges. None of this is OT equipment in the ISA-95 sense, and none of it will arrive through an ICS advisory feed. It is, however, the layer that carries plant traffic to the data centre, terminates the site-to-site links between facilities, and in a great many networks enforces the segmentation that the whole OT security programme is resting on. That makes it the practical companion to the Fire Ant research elsewhere on this page, which documents a China-nexus actor operating from compromised Cisco IOS XR routers and TACACS servers precisely because they sit outside OT monitoring. - Cisco security advisories — reported by SecurityWeek and cross-checked against the Cisco PSIRT advisory index - Published 3 Sep 2026 — verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [Medium] Britain moves to take the power to disconnect your suppliers — and a four-day generator outage is what tabled the amendment
item.category: UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill — Supplier designation powers, UK
item.description: Late amendments to the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill would give ministers power to stop critical-sector organisations using technology suppliers judged high risk. The Bill was introduced in November 2025, has cleared the Commons and sits in the Lords as HL Bill 32, close to Royal Assent; the amendments were tabled on 24 August, two days after reporting that Iran-linked actors had forced a small UK generating site offline for four days (see Incidents & Attacks). The approach is a departure worth noting: rather than only demanding better in-house security from operators, it lets government cut them off from third parties it considers inadequately secured, regardless of the supplier’s size or sector. The Bill already carries strict incident-reporting timelines and heavy penalties. Practitioners quoted in the coverage make the obvious point — a small integrator or managed service provider with standing remote access into a plant may not think of itself as critical national infrastructure, but a designation regime will decide that for it.

item.title: [Medium] The companion to “prepare to disconnect”: agencies publish what to say, and to whom, while the plant is still down
item.category: Joint guidance — CISA, FBI and international partners; communicating during IT and OT outages
item.description: On 3 September CISA, the FBI and international partners published joint guidance on how service providers should plan and deliver communications during IT and OT outages — defined notification thresholds and audiences, plain-language status updates, and root-cause detail written for the people who have to keep operating. It is deliberately unglamorous, and it fills the gap left by this summer’s isolation guidance: CI Fortify told operators to be able to cut the connection and run without it, and this tells them what customers, regulators and dependent operators hear while that is happening. The guidance is non-binding, but the clocks around it are not — the EU Cyber Resilience Act’s 24-hour early warning starts on 11 September, and CIRCIA, NIS2 and TSA reporting obligations all run on their own timers during exactly the window this document addresses. - SecurityWeek reporting on the tabled amendments, read against the UK government’s Cyber Security and Resilience Bill collection on gov.uk - Amendments tabled 24 Aug 2026; reported 2 Sep 2026; Bill awaiting Royal Assent — verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [Medium] A six-month federal pilot will red-team Texas water utilities — and it is meant to become a template
item.category: Policy — Federal/state water cyber pilot; red-teaming, no-cost tooling
item.description: The White House Office of the National Cyber Director, the EPA, CISA and Texas Cyber Command launched Project Watershed 250 on 31 August, a six-month pilot that will stress-test water utility networks in Texas with red-team exercises and provide participating systems with federal, state and vendor-supplied cyber defences at no cost. Microsoft, Palo Alto Networks, Dragos, Tenable, Forescout and Reflection AI are named among the participants. The administration says the pilot is not a response to the July intrusions that affected more than 30 Minnesota water systems, though it acknowledges those incidents underscored the exposure; officials frame it as a scalable model to extend nationally if it works. The reason this matters beyond Texas is the design assumption behind it, stated plainly by the participants: the sector’s roughly 150,000 systems are mostly small, thinly staffed and cannot be turned into enterprise security organisations, so the intervention has to be visibility and prioritisation delivered from outside rather than headcount hired inside. Whatever the pilot publishes about what the red teams actually found will be the more valuable output — CISA’s own red-team assessments at two critical-infrastructure organisations, released a week earlier, showed one failing to detect initial access and lateral movement entirely. - Office of the National Cyber Director / Texas Cyber Command announcement, with EPA and CISA as federal partners — as reported by Industrial Cyber and Fox News Digital; vendor participation confirmed by Tenable, Microsoft, Dragos and Forescout statements - Announced 31 Aug 2026; reported 1 Sep 2026 — verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [Medium] In one week, anyone selling a connected product into the EU owes a 24-hour warning on exploited vulnerabilities
item.category: EU Cyber Resilience Act — Reporting obligations effective 11 Sep 2026
item.description: The EU Cyber Resilience Act enters its reporting phase on 11 September 2026. From that date, manufacturers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents affecting their products, with an early warning inside 24 hours and a fuller notification inside 72 hours. The scope reaches far past consumer IoT: PLCs, RTUs, drives, gateways, HMIs, protocol converters and the engineering software around them are products with digital elements, and the obligation follows the manufacturer regardless of where the affected device is installed. Legal analysts advise naming an owner now and building the assessment, escalation and customer-communication path in advance, coordinating it with existing NIS2 and GDPR duties rather than standing up a third parallel process. - Freshfields analysis via Lexology, surfaced in the Viakoo/Security Boulevard daily OT briefing - Analysis published 1 Sep 2026; obligations effective 11 Sep 2026 (forward-looking) — verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET

item.title: [Medium] “Prepare to disconnect” is now written guidance — and it assumes you can run the plant for months without IT
item.category: Five Eyes guidance — ASD/ACSC, CISA, FBI, NCSC‑UK, CCCS; OT isolation readiness
item.description: The Five Eyes agencies’ CI Fortify — Advice for isolating vital systems, published 28 July and pushed back into the OT conversation on 2 September by vendor analyses from Nozomi, OPSWAT and Zscaler, sets out a six-step path to being able to cut vital OT loose from everything else and keep delivering service. The steps are unglamorous and in order: identify vital systems and networks; identify your critical customers and set a service target in real units — megawatts, million gallons per day; group hosts by criticality and trust; map every interconnection and pick your isolation points; build separation that actually holds; then write and test a graduated isolation plan. The part practitioners keep returning to is the dependency list. The guidance names the shared services that quietly defeat isolation — Active Directory, DNS and DHCP, PKI and certificate services, NTP/PTP time sync, shared hypervisors and SANs, backup and recovery, and the routing and switching fabric itself — and says operators must eliminate those dependencies, not document them. It is blunt about carrier links too: treat any carrier-provided service as untrusted and potentially hostile, encrypt with a dedicated device rather than the crypto built into an OT product, and manage that device only from inside the OT domain. That advice reads differently after CERT Polska’s private-APN case (see Incidents & Attacks), which is the failure mode this paragraph exists to prevent. - ASD/ACSC with CISA, FBI, NCSC‑UK, NCSC‑NZ and CCCS, CI Fortify — Advice for isolating vital systems (read in full via ic3.gov) — returned to circulation by Nozomi Networks, OPSWAT and Zscaler analyses and the Viakoo/Security Boulevard daily OT briefing - Guidance published 28 Jul 2026; re-surfaced by vendor analysis 2 Sep 2026 — primary source read and verified 4 Sep 2026, 6:18 PM ET
